narrative:
The model predicted a 63.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the first decile (bottom 10%) of your class in Year 3 is well below the average of roughly the fifth or sixth decile among students who were accepted. This low ranking signaled to the model a higher risk of struggling with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score of 36 was the second most important factor. Although this score is only slightly below the 37.2 average of accepted students, it still nudged the prediction mildly toward passing rather than failing.

Your first-year class ranking came third. Being in the second decile in Year 1 also pulled the outcome toward failure, though less powerfully than your third-year performance.

Taken together, the model saw your consistently low class rankings as the dominant signal outweighing the relatively solid LSAT and undergraduate GPA of 3.0.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your academic record. Retaking courses to improve your GPA, gaining targeted bar-prep experience, or applying to schools with different admissions models could improve your chances in a future cycle. Consider speaking with an admissions counselor about how to address these specific weaknesses in your next application.
